confidence_interval.rationale: The paper makes genuine contributions in problem formulation, system design, and empirical study, but critical claims lack quantitative evidence and direct empirical comparison to baselines. The metric discrepancy (74.7% vs. 77.9%) is unexplained and undermines credibility. Grammar induction precision is claimed but not measured. Cross-user generalization is claimed but not explicitly measured. Transferability is speculative. The work is technically sound but empirically incomplete. Confidence is moderate (55–75%) reflecting genuine novelty and solid system design offset by significant evaluation gaps. If the metric discrepancy is resolved, grammar induction precision is validated, and cross-user generalization is measured, confidence would increase to 70–85%. If transferability is empirically demonstrated, confidence would increase to 75–90%.

consensus_findings: The paper introduces a novel conceptual frame ('naturalization') for incrementally extending a programming language through user-provided definitions in a community setting. This is a genuine divergence from prior work (Wang et al. 2016, GENLEX) and represents a coherent contribution to interactive machine learning and semantic parsing.

The core algorithmic contribution—grammar induction via highest-scoring maximal packings optimized by a semantic parsing model—is principled and well-motivated. The counterexample (Eq. 2) effectively demonstrates why greedy heuristics fail, and the dynamic programming solution is sound.

The system design (Voxelurn) is pragmatic and well-executed. The core language balances expressivity with usability through thoughtful design choices (scoping mechanism, selection-based interface, lambda DCS). Users successfully built 230 complex structures, demonstrating practical viability.

The empirical study is ambitious in scale: 70 qualified workers, 42 participants, 230 structures, 64,075 utterances, 2,495 definitions over 3 days. This provides credible evidence that community-driven language naturalization is feasible at scale.

Critical evaluation gaps exist across multiple dimensions: (1) no quantitative precision/recall metrics for grammar induction despite 'high precision' claims; (2) no direct empirical comparison of definitions vs. weak supervision vs. demonstrations on learning efficiency; (3) cross-user generalization claimed but not explicitly measured; (4) metric discrepancy (74.7% vs. 77.9%) unexplained; (5) alignment heuristics are ad-hoc with no ablation or precision analysis; (6) three modes of naturalization are post-hoc categorization without quantitative validation; (7) expressiveness measured by proxy without direct validation; (8) transferability entirely speculative.

Selection bias (42 of 70 qualified workers participated) and potential confounds from incentive structure (leaderboard, prizes, citations) raise concerns about generalizability and interpretation of adoption metrics. No analysis of these effects is provided.

The paper is internally coherent and logically sound, but the empirical validation does not match the boldness of the conceptual claims. The work demonstrates technical competence in system design and algorithmic contribution, but lacks the rigorous evaluation needed to fully support the main claims.

The paper makes incremental but meaningful contributions to interactive machine learning and semantic parsing. The novelty is primarily in the combination of existing techniques (semantic parsing, grammar induction, online learning) applied to a novel supervision signal (definitions) in a community-driven setting, rather than in fundamental algorithmic innovation.
disagreements: Reviewer 1 (structure_analyst) emphasizes logical coherence and identifies where the argument chain is strong (system design, problem formulation) vs. weak (missing empirical evidence at critical junctures). Reviewer 4 (novelty_assessor_disruptive) treats sparse precedent as a possible innovation signal and emphasizes the conceptual novelty of the naturalization frame, while Reviewer 3 (novelty_assessor_incremental) views the contribution as incremental refinement rather than disruptive innovation. This reflects different weightings of conceptual novelty vs. empirical rigor.

Reviewer 2 (methodology_auditor) prioritizes reproducibility and validity, flagging methodological gaps as major concerns. Reviewer 5 (claim_verifier) operates in evidence-and-uncertainty-first mode and distinguishes supported from unsupported claims. Both identify similar gaps but with different emphasis: Reviewer 2 focuses on what is missing (precision metrics, baselines, cross-user generalization measurement), while Reviewer 5 focuses on the gap between claims and evidence.

Reviewers disagree on the severity of the metric discrepancy (74.7% vs. 77.9%). Reviewer 1 and 2 flag it as a major concern undermining credibility of the main empirical claim. Reviewer 5 treats it as critical but potentially resolvable. Reviewer 4 acknowledges it but focuses more on the conceptual novelty. The discrepancy is unexplained in the manuscript, making it difficult to assess whether it reflects a typo, different metric definitions, or data reporting error.

Reviewers differ on how to interpret the adoption metric (74.7% in last 10K utterances). Reviewer 1 notes it conflates 'induced' with 'naturalized' and lacks baseline. Reviewer 2 emphasizes selection bias and incentive effects. Reviewer 4 treats it as evidence of practical utility despite methodological gaps. Reviewer 5 notes the metric is meaningful but incomplete without analysis of rule quality distribution. The disagreement reflects different standards for what constitutes sufficient evidence of 'adoption'.

Reviewer 4 (disruptive lens) emphasizes that the paper challenges established paradigms in semantic parsing and has high disruptive potential despite incomplete empirical validation. Reviewer 3 (incremental lens) views the contribution as incremental refinement of existing paradigms. This reflects different perspectives on novelty: whether the work is fundamentally new (disruptive) or a meaningful extension of existing ideas (incremental).
uncertainty_hotspots: Metric discrepancy (74.7% vs. 77.9%): The abstract and text report different adoption rates for the same metric (last 10K utterances). This is unexplained and raises questions about data accuracy or metric definition. Unclear which figure is correct or if both are valid for different subsets of data.

Grammar induction precision: The paper claims 'high precision' for induced rules but provides no quantitative metrics (precision, recall, F1). No comparison to GENLEX or higher-order unification on same definitions. Unclear if highest-scoring packings actually achieve higher precision than alternatives.

Cross-user generalization: The paper claims rules 'immediately generalize across users' but does not explicitly measure cross-user generalization. Citation tracking system exists but statistics are not reported. Unclear if rules authored by user A are actually used by user B or if adoption is primarily user-specific.

Alignment heuristics: The exclusion and projectivity heuristics are presented without principled justification or ablation study. Unclear how often heuristics trigger, how often they produce correct vs. spurious rules, or whether they are necessary for system performance.

Three modes of naturalization: Table 3 categorizes definitions into three modes (short forms, syntactic variations, higher-level concepts) but provides no quantitative distribution, inter-rater reliability, or statistical validation. Unclear if three modes are exhaustive or if other patterns exist.

Expressiveness growth: Program-to-utterance ratio is used as a proxy for expressiveness, but no direct measure of concept complexity is provided. Unclear if ratio increase reflects genuine expressiveness growth or confounds (user familiarity, verbose definitions, short forms reducing denominator).

Selection bias and incentive effects: 42 of 70 qualified workers participated; no analysis of non-participants. Leaderboard, prizes, and citations may artificially inflate adoption; unclear if adoption persists without incentives. Sensitivity to these confounds is unknown.

Transferability: The paper claims the methodology 'should apply' to databases, regex, robot instructions, but provides no empirical validation. Voxelurn has specific affordances (visual feedback, spatial structure) that may not transfer. Unclear which domain properties are necessary for naturalization to succeed.

Online learning stability: The model is updated online via AdaGrad but no analysis of convergence, stability, or catastrophic forgetting is provided. Unclear if model remains stable over 70K utterances or if early rules are downweighted over time.

Feature importance: The semantic parsing model uses ~5 + #rules + #users + #users^2 + V^4 × #cats + 3 + 3×#users features but no ablation study shows which features are important. Unclear if social features (author, friends) are necessary or if they overfit.
model_diversity_effects: Structure_analyst (Reviewer 1) prioritizes logical coherence and identifies where the argument chain is strong vs. weak. This role naturally emphasizes the gap between claims and evidence, leading to identification of critical junctures where empirical validation is missing (precision metrics, cross-user generalization measurement, baseline comparisons).

Methodology_auditor (Reviewer 2) prioritizes reproducibility and validity, flagging methodological gaps as major concerns. This role naturally emphasizes what is missing (precision metrics, baselines, ablation studies) and how to address gaps through additional experiments or analysis.

Novelty_assessor_incremental (Reviewer 3) views the contribution through an incremental-refinement lens, emphasizing that the work extends existing paradigms (interactive learning, grammar induction) in a meaningful but not disruptive way. This role naturally leads to assessment of whether the novelty is sufficient given the evaluation rigor.

Novelty_assessor_disruptive (Reviewer 4) views the contribution through a disruptive-thinking lens, treating sparse precedent as a possible innovation signal and emphasizing the conceptual novelty of the naturalization frame. This role naturally leads to protection of unconventional ideas from being penalized for divergence from mainstream literature.

Claim_verifier (Reviewer 5) operates in evidence-and-uncertainty-first mode, distinguishing supported from unsupported claims and flagging uncertainty rather than rendering binary verdicts. This role naturally emphasizes the gap between claims and evidence and identifies which claims are well-supported vs. speculative.

The diversity of roles produces complementary perspectives: structure_analyst identifies logical gaps, methodology_auditor identifies empirical gaps, novelty_assessors assess novelty from different lenses, and claim_verifier cross-checks claims against evidence. Together, they provide a comprehensive assessment of the paper's strengths and weaknesses.

Role-specific effects are most pronounced in assessment of novelty and transferability: disruptive lens (Reviewer 4) treats these more favorably than incremental lens (Reviewer 3), reflecting different standards for what constitutes sufficient novelty. However, all reviewers agree on the core methodological gaps (missing precision metrics, no direct comparisons, selection bias).
meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper makes genuine contributions to interactive machine learning and semantic parsing through a novel conceptual frame (naturalization) and a well-designed system (Voxelurn). The core ideas are sound and the empirical study is ambitious. However, critical claims lack quantitative evidence and direct empirical comparison to baselines. The paper is suitable for publication with major revisions addressing: (1) the metric discrepancy (74.7% vs. 77.9%) must be resolved and explained; (2) grammar induction precision must be quantified via manual evaluation and compared to GENLEX and higher-order unification; (3) cross-user generalization must be explicitly measured (e.g., rules authored by user A used by user B); (4) alignment heuristics must be ablated and precision-analyzed; (5) three modes of naturalization must be quantified and validated; (6) expressiveness must be measured directly, not via proxy; (7) selection bias and incentive effects must be analyzed; (8) transferability must be reframed as future work or empirically demonstrated in at least one other domain. The paper would also benefit from: (1) direct empirical comparison of definitions vs. weak supervision vs. demonstrations on learning efficiency; (2) analysis of rule quality distribution and adoption by rule quality; (3) scalability metrics (parsing time, memory, chart size); (4) feature ablation study; (5) online learning stability analysis. These revisions would significantly strengthen the paper and address the gap between the boldness of the conceptual claims and the completeness of the empirical validation.
meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper introduces a novel and well-motivated approach to language naturalization through community-driven definition-based grammar induction. The system design is pragmatic and the user study is ambitious. To strengthen the paper, address the following critical issues: (1) Resolve the metric discrepancy (74.7% vs. 77.9%) by clarifying which figure is correct and explaining any differences. (2) Quantify grammar induction precision: manually evaluate a sample of induced rules (100-200) and report precision, recall, F1. Compare to GENLEX and higher-order unification on the same definitions. (3) Measure cross-user generalization explicitly: report citation statistics (distribution of citations per rule, % of rules cited by non-authors, success rate of cross-user rule usage). (4) Conduct direct empirical comparison of definitions vs. weak supervision vs. demonstrations on learning efficiency (learning curves, sample complexity). (5) Ablate alignment heuristics: measure system performance with and without alignment-based extension, and report precision/recall of alignment-based rules. (6) Quantify the three modes of naturalization: report count and percentage of definitions in each mode, conduct inter-rater reliability study, analyze temporal evolution. (7) Validate expressiveness metric: measure concept complexity directly (not via proxy), compare to baseline (core language only), analyze whether ratio increase is driven by short forms or higher-level concepts. (8) Analyze selection bias and incentive effects: report reasons for non-participation, conduct sensitivity analysis on adoption metrics, measure adoption with and without incentives. (9) Reframe transferability as future work or conduct pilot studies in at least one other domain. (10) Provide quantitative scalability metrics (parsing time, memory, chart size as function of rule count). These revisions will address the gap between your conceptual contributions and empirical validation, significantly strengthening the paper.
transparency_report: This meta-review synthesizes five specialist reviews operating under different cognitive roles and epistemic variants: structure_analyst (logical-coherence-first), methodology_auditor (reproducibility-and-validity-first), novelty_assessor_incremental (incremental-contribution lens), novelty_assessor_disruptive (disruptive-thinking lens), and claim_verifier (evidence-and-uncertainty-first). Each reviewer brings a distinct perspective on the paper's contributions and limitations.

The specialist reviews identify consistent patterns of agreement and disagreement. All reviewers agree on core methodological gaps: missing precision metrics for grammar induction, no direct empirical comparison to baselines, selection bias (42/70 participants), metric discrepancy (74.7% vs. 77.9%), and lack of explicit measurement of cross-user generalization. These gaps are flagged as major concerns across all reviews.

Disagreements emerge primarily in assessment of novelty and how to weigh conceptual contributions against empirical validation. The disruptive lens (Reviewer 4) emphasizes the conceptual novelty of the naturalization frame and treats sparse precedent as a possible innovation signal. The incremental lens (Reviewer 3) views the contribution as meaningful but incremental refinement of existing paradigms. The structure_analyst (Reviewer 1) focuses on logical coherence and identifies where the argument chain is strong vs. weak. The methodology_auditor (Reviewer 2) prioritizes reproducibility and flags what is missing. The claim_verifier (Reviewer 5) distinguishes supported from unsupported claims and flags uncertainty.

The retrieved literature corpus (external Q1/Q2 articles) did not return highly relevant papers on interactive language learning or community-driven language evolution. The most relevant papers (Wang et al. 2016, GENLEX, higher-order unification) are cited in the manuscript itself. This suggests either sparse coverage in the corpus or indexing gaps. The absence of close analogs in the retrieved corpus is consistent with the paper's novelty claim and is treated as a possible innovation signal rather than automatic weakness.

Reviewer guidelines (ARR Reviewer Guidelines) emphasize technical soundness, appropriate scoping, avoiding common NLP paper problems (missing baselines, incomplete evaluation), and distinguishing novelty from validity. All specialist reviews apply these standards and identify similar gaps in evaluation rigor.

The paper's main claims (C1-C9) form a logical chain: definitions enable learning (C1) → community can teach simultaneously (C2) → rapid adoption (C6) → expressiveness grows (C7). However, critical links in this chain lack empirical validation: C1 lacks direct comparison to weak supervision; C2 lacks explicit measurement of cross-user generalization; C6 contains a metric discrepancy; C7 uses a proxy measure without validation.

The paper demonstrates technical soundness in system design and algorithmic contribution, but the empirical validation does not match the boldness of the conceptual claims. This is a common pattern in novel work: the idea is ahead of the evaluation. The paper would be significantly strengthened by addressing the evaluation gaps identified by all reviewers.

Confidence intervals reported by individual reviewers range from 0.45-0.75 (Reviewer 2), 0.55-0.75 (Reviewer 1), 0.55-0.75 (Reviewer 3), 0.55-0.75 (Reviewer 4), and 0.55-0.75 (Reviewer 5). The consensus confidence interval is approximately 0.55-0.75, reflecting moderate uncertainty due to evaluation gaps offset by genuine novelty and solid system design.
epistemic_limits: The meta-review cannot definitively resolve the metric discrepancy (74.7% vs. 77.9%) without access to the raw data and metric definitions. Both figures are reported in the manuscript, but the discrepancy is unexplained. The true adoption rate could be either value, or both could be correct for different subsets of data.

The meta-review cannot assess grammar induction precision without manual evaluation of induced rules. The paper claims 'high precision' but provides no quantitative metrics. The true precision could be high (>90%), moderate (70-90%), or low (<70%), but this cannot be determined from the manuscript alone.

The meta-review cannot measure cross-user generalization without access to citation statistics and rule usage data. The paper mentions a citation tracking system but does not report statistics. The true extent of cross-user generalization could be high (>50% of rules used by multiple users), moderate (20-50%), or low (<20%), but this cannot be determined from the manuscript alone.

The meta-review cannot assess the impact of incentive structure (leaderboard, prizes, citations) on adoption without a control condition or follow-up study. The true effect of incentives could be large (adoption would be much lower without incentives), moderate, or small (adoption would persist without incentives), but this cannot be determined from the manuscript alone.

The meta-review cannot validate the three modes of naturalization without quantitative analysis and inter-rater reliability study. The true distribution of definitions across modes could be balanced (33% each), skewed (e.g., 50% short forms, 30% syntactic variations, 20% higher-level concepts), or follow a different pattern entirely, but this cannot be determined from the manuscript alone.

The meta-review cannot assess transferability to other domains without empirical validation. The paper claims the methodology 'should apply' to databases, regex, robot instructions, but provides no evidence. The true transferability could be high (methodology works well in other domains), moderate (requires domain-specific adaptations), or low (methodology is specific to voxel worlds), but this cannot be determined from the manuscript alone.

The meta-review cannot assess online learning stability without analysis of model parameters and performance over time. The paper does not report convergence, stability, or potential for catastrophic forgetting. The true stability could be high (model converges and remains stable), moderate (model exhibits some drift), or low (model becomes unstable or overfits to recent users), but this cannot be determined from the manuscript alone.

The meta-review operates under the assumption that the manuscript accurately reports the empirical results. If there are errors in data collection, analysis, or reporting, the assessment would be affected. The metric discrepancy (74.7% vs. 77.9%) raises questions about data accuracy, but without access to raw data, this cannot be verified.

The meta-review cannot assess the generalizability of results to populations beyond the 42 AMT workers who participated. The selection bias (42 of 70 qualified workers participated) limits generalizability, but the true extent of bias cannot be determined without analyzing non-participants.

The meta-review is limited by the scope of the retrieved literature corpus. If there are relevant papers on interactive language learning or community-driven language evolution that are not in the corpus, the novelty assessment could be affected. The absence of close analogs in the retrieved corpus is consistent with the paper's novelty claim, but this is not definitive.

human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper makes genuine contributions to interactive machine learning and semantic parsing through a novel conceptual frame (naturalization) and well-designed system (Voxelurn). The core ideas are sound and the empirical study is ambitious. However, critical claims lack quantitative evidence and direct empirical comparison to baselines. The paper is suitable for publication with major revisions addressing the following: (1) Resolve the metric discrepancy (74.7% vs. 77.9%) by clarifying which figure is correct and explaining any differences. (2) Quantify grammar induction precision via manual evaluation of 100-200 induced rules; compare to GENLEX and higher-order unification on same definitions. (3) Explicitly measure cross-user generalization: report citation statistics and success rate of cross-user rule usage. (4) Conduct direct empirical comparison of definitions vs. weak supervision vs. demonstrations on learning efficiency (learning curves, sample complexity). (5) Ablate alignment heuristics: measure system performance with and without alignment-based extension; report precision/recall of alignment-based rules. (6) Quantify three modes of naturalization: report distribution across modes, conduct inter-rater reliability study, analyze temporal evolution. (7) Validate expressiveness metric: measure concept complexity directly (not via proxy); compare to baseline (core language only). (8) Analyze selection bias and incentive effects: report reasons for non-participation, conduct sensitivity analysis on adoption metrics, measure adoption with and without incentives. (9) Reframe transferability as future work or conduct pilot studies in at least one other domain. (10) Provide quantitative scalability metrics (parsing time, memory, chart size as function of rule count). These revisions will address the gap between conceptual contributions and empirical validation, significantly strengthening the paper for publication.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper introduces a novel and well-motivated approach to language naturalization through community-driven definition-based grammar induction. The system design is pragmatic and the user study is ambitious. To strengthen the paper and address reviewer concerns, prioritize the following revisions: (1) CRITICAL: Resolve the metric discrepancy (74.7% vs. 77.9%) by clarifying which figure is correct and explaining any differences in metric definition or data subset. (2) Quantify grammar induction precision: manually evaluate 100-200 induced rules and report precision, recall, F1; compare to GENLEX and higher-order unification on same definitions. (3) Measure cross-user generalization explicitly: report citation statistics (distribution of citations per rule, % of rules cited by non-authors, success rate of cross-user rule usage). (4) Conduct direct empirical comparison of definitions vs. weak supervision vs. demonstrations: measure learning curves (accuracy vs. number of examples) for each supervision type. (5) Ablate alignment heuristics: measure system performance with and without alignment-based extension; report precision/recall of alignment-based rules; justify heuristic choices. (6) Quantify three modes of naturalization: report count and percentage of definitions in each mode; conduct inter-rater reliability study (Cohen's kappa); analyze temporal evolution. (7) Validate expressiveness metric: measure concept complexity directly (semantic similarity, program depth, abstraction level); compare to baseline (core language only); analyze whether ratio increase driven by short forms or higher-level concepts. (8) Analyze selection bias and incentive effects: report reasons for non-participation; conduct sensitivity analysis (how would adoption metrics change if non-participants had participated?); measure adoption with and without incentives. (9) Reframe transferability as future work or conduct pilot studies in at least one other domain (e.g., regex or database queries). (10) Provide quantitative scalability metrics: parsing time, memory usage, chart size as function of rule count. These revisions will address the gap between your conceptual contributions and empirical validation, significantly strengthening the paper.

We used the owl verbalizer of the swat project (Stevens et al., 2011; Williams, Third, & Power, 2011), which we found to be particularly robust and useful. 24 The verbal- izer produces an alphabetical glossary with an entry for each named class, property, and individual, without requiring domain-dependent generation resources. Each glossary entry is a sequence of English-like sentences expressing the corresponding owl statements of the ontology. The swat verbalizer uses a predetermined partial order of statements in each glossary entry; for example, when describing a class, statements about equivalent classes or super-classes are mentioned ﬁrst, and individuals belonging in the target class are men- tioned last. 25 The verbalizer actually translates the owl ontology to Prolog, it extracts lexicon entries from owl identiﬁers and rdfs:label strings, and it uses predetermined sen- tence plans speciﬁed as a dcg grammar. It also aggregates, in eﬀect, message triples of the same property that share one argument ( S or O) (Williams & Power, 2010). Our hypothesis was that the domain-dependent generation resources would help Natu- ralowl produce texts that end-users would consider more ﬂuent and coherent, compared to those produced by the swat verbalizer, but also those produced by Natural owl without domain-dependent generation resources. In addition, many programming languages for cognitive agents embed knowledge rep- resentation (KR) languages like Prolog or a Web Ontology Language (OWL). Some agent programming languages also embed (instead of extend) an object-oriented programming lan- guage such as Java. This introduces the additional problem of how to employ the debugging frameworks that are available for the embedded languages. For example, the SWI Prolog trace mechanism could be made available through the Goal debugger in some way. Finally, the debugger design should be evaluated on different groups of users, i.e., different from novice (ﬁrst-year student) programmers. Moreover, additional quantitative measures such as the average time of ﬁnding a bug, the average quality of programs (e.g., the amount of faults/failures in a result with or without use of the source-level debugger), and more could give more insights into the challenges of debugging multi-agent systems. top_documents.title: Document 4
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
